system: Egyptian hours — the twelve hours of the night and the twelve of the day. Two distinct bodies of material are recorded here and NOT merged: (a) the twelve Divisions of the Tuat in the Book Am-Tuat, which Budge reports the Egyptians regarded as hours, each with a region-name, a gate-name and in most cases an hour-goddess; (b) Egyptian timekeeping proper — decan-star risings and the month-scaled water clock. The Am-Tuat is a funerary cosmography, not a civil timetable, and nothing here licenses presenting it as one.
scopeNote: THIS SYSTEM HAS NO RULER COLUMN. The Am-Tuat hour-goddesses are the hours' own names and tutelary figures inside a funerary book; they are not lords of a rotating planetary sequence and no source in this ledger treats them as such. Round 1 of this project filled a ruler column with those goddesses; that column is empty here by maintainer ruling and by the ledger's own evidence (see rulerColumnJustification). Separately: the repo's assets/js/core/planetary-hours.js implements the Hellenistic/Chaldean planetary-hour rotation, which is a different system with a different pedigree, and it must not be relabelled 'Egyptian' on the strength of Cassius Dio's second-hand attribution (S6).
rulerColumnJustification: FALSE, on four independent lines of ledger evidence, none of which is an argument from silence alone. (1) BUDGE SETS THE TWO SERIES SIDE BY SIDE AND NEVER JOINS THEM. In Gods of the Egyptians II (1904) ch. XIX, §XI and §XII give twelve-name deity lists for the hours of the night and of the day; §XIII, on the immediately following page, gives the planets and their gods — Jupiter is recorded as having no god at all, Saturn's god is Horus, and the other three are Ra, Set and Osiris. Two non-intersecting series on facing pages; no planet is assigned to any hour anywhere in the chapter. [S4-g, S4-h, S4-i] (2) THE ONE EGYPTIAN CORPUS WHERE HOUR-LORDS WOULD BE MOST EXPECTED DOES NOT HAVE THEM. The Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden (Griffith & Thompson 1904) — a Roman-period operative magical text — uses hours as bare clock-times ('until the time of the seventh hour of the day'; 'at the time of the third hour(?) of evening') and separately invokes planets ('O water-drawing of the planet Jupiter'), and never joins the two. The fetcher's whole-file counts: 'hour' 13, 'planet' 3, 'Saturn' 1 and that one in a modern editorial cross-reference. [S5-a, S5-b, S5-c, S5-e, S5-d] (3) BUDGE'S AM-TUAT VOLUME NAMES EXACTLY ONE PLANET, AS AN IMAGE. At the door into the Sixth Division he notes 'the large five-rayed star which is the symbol of the planet Venus' — a figure in a register, not a ruler of anything. [S1-d] (4) THE ONE ANCIENT TEXT THAT ATTACHES HOUR-RULERS TO THE WORD 'EGYPTIANS' NAMES NO EGYPTIAN HOUR. Cassius Dio 37.18–19 credits the planetary week to the Egyptians and gives the hour-rotation that generates it — begin at the first hour, assign the first to Saturn, follow the order of the cycles the Egyptians observe — but Dio writes in the early third century AD, calls the practice comparatively recent, says the ancient Greeks never understood it, and names no Egyptian hour, no Egyptian hour-name and no Egyptian source. That is an attribution reported at second hand in Greek in the Roman imperial period; it is evidence about the Hellenistic-Roman planetary week, not about a pharaonic Egyptian hour-lord table. [S6-a, S6-b, S6-c, S6-d] CONSEQUENTLY: the `ruler` property is omitted from every entry in this dossier rather than being written as 'none' or 'unattested'. An empty column is the finding. Do not render one.
dayStart: UNSETTLED, AND THREE DIFFERENT BOUNDARIES ARE IN PLAY. A page that picks one and calls it 'the Egyptian day start' asserts something no source in this ledger asserts. (1) THE CIVIL DAY BEGINS AT DAWN. Parker, The Calendars of Ancient Egypt (SAOC 26, Chicago 1950), §32, holds that the Egyptian civil day opened at daybreak and that each such day ran to the following daybreak, and treats the point as already settled rather than re-arguing it. His footnote — notes to ch. II, n. 26 — rests that on three earlier scholars (an 'op. cit.' at pp. 101–2, Lepsius at pp. 130–31, and Sethe's Zeitrechnung pp. 130–38). So the dawn boundary as this dossier holds it is Parker REPORTING a prior demonstration, not Parker demonstrating one. [S8-a, S8-b] (2) PARKER HIMSELF RECORDS TWO BOUNDARIES INSIDE ONE CIVILISATION. His notes to ch. I, n. 17, on the word hd-tꜣ: in the astronomical day the pre-sunrise light belongs to the PRECEDING day; in the ordinary day of people who were up before sunrise it is simply daybreak of the NEW day. Two day-boundaries, on Parker's own account, unreconciled here. [S8-d] (3) TWO ROUTES TO THE MORNING BOUNDARY, BOTH KEPT. Parker quotes Sethe in German at §33 — the year began with the pre-dawn first visibility of Sirius, so the start of the day must fall in the morning — then rejects Sethe's premise that any such 'Normaljahr' existed while retaining the morning start. [S8-c] (4) THE NIGHT-HOUR COUNT IS ANCHORED AT SUNSET, NOT AT DAWN. Parker §208: the Karnak clepsydra of Amenhotep III was topped up completely at sundown, and night hour two started once the water level had sunk as far as the opening mark on that month's own scale. The instrument starts the night count at sunset regardless of where the civil date turns over. [S8-e, S8-f] (5) NOTHING IN THIS LEDGER STATES OUTRIGHT THAT THE TWELVE DAY-HOURS BEGIN AT SUNRISE. The nearest is second-hand: Brack-Bernsen (BMCR 2020.11.44), reviewing Down to the Hour, reports Schomberg arguing that eleven markers suffice for twelve hours because by the close of the twelfth the sun is already up, or already down. That implies sunrise and sunset as the outer bounds of the two twelve-hour series, but it is a reviewer's report of a chapter this ledger could not obtain, and it is recorded as such. [S10-f]
divisionRule: TWELVE HOURS OF NIGHT AND TWELVE OF DAY. THE DIVISION INTO TWELVE IS ATTESTED. DIVISION INTO TWELVE *EQUAL* PARTS IS NOT. What the ledger supports: · TWELVE, AND OF VARYING LENGTH THROUGH THE YEAR. Ainsworth (MA research essay, Queen's University, 2018), p. 2, holds that the night in Egypt carried twelve hours whose length shifted with the season; her authority is footnote 3 to Dodd, JRASC 99.2 (2005), p. 67. Reported at second hand, and tiered accordingly. [S9-a, S9-c] · THE TWELVE TUAT DIVISIONS ARE HOURS. Budge, Egyptian Heaven and Hell III (1906), p. 94: the Egyptians regarded each of the twelve divisions as the equivalent of an hour. Budge raises the obvious objection himself — that in an Egyptian summer the night is not twelve hours long — and answers it by treating divisions I and XII as ante-chambers rather than true Tuat. Both the objection and that answer are his, and the answer is theological rather than astronomical. [S3-b, S3-c] · THE NIGHT HOURS WERE READ OFF AN INSTRUMENT, NOT COMPUTED. Parker §208: the vessel is filled at sunset and each hour begins when the water reaches the next mark of the scale for that civil month — twelve month-scales, one per month. Brack-Bernsen reports von Lieven and Schomberg to the same effect: the vessel carried one row of interior holes per civil month, and the night hour then in progress was found from the row belonging to that month. A table, not an arithmetic. [S8-e, S8-f, S10-c] · THE DECANS DID NOT PRODUCE EQUAL INTERVALS. Brack-Bernsen reports Symons demonstrating that no set of real stars can both make its first dawn appearance on the required day and also come up at evenly spaced moments — so what the decans marked out through the night were stretches of UNEQUAL length. Ainsworth adds that the transit-decan instruments are unlikely to have served the living for telling time as it passed, falling short of the natural year by five and a quarter days, and that the star charts were set for particular moments and served the dead. [S10-a, S10-b, S9-b, S9-d] · A RATIO IS ON THE RECORD. Parker's notes to ch. V, n. 73, report Borchardt's proportion between longest and shortest scale — fourteen fingers against twelve — as matching the Karnak vessel precisely. [S8-i] · WHICH MONTH CARRIES THE SHORTEST NIGHT IS CONTESTED. Parker §208 makes the shortest scale II šmw (printed '9mw' by the extraction; the tenth civil month) and the longest IIII ꜣḫt, and concludes that the vessel therefore gives no evidence whatever for a fixed Sothic year; Brack-Bernsen reports Schomberg placing the summer solstice, hence the shortest night, in month 9, which would push the Karnak vessel's date back by roughly 250 years. Both positions stand. [S8-g, S8-h, S10-d, S10-e] · HOURS WERE REAL APPOINTMENT TIMES. Parker §294 quotes the Dendera calendar timing a processional appearance of Hathor to the arrival of the third hour; Brugsch's preface material dates the Sirius epoch to the eleventh hour of the night of the fifth epagomenal day. [S8-l, S7-c] · THE DAY SIDE HAS NEITHER ARITHMETIC NOR INSTRUMENT IN THIS LEDGER — see gaps[3]. CONSEQUENCE FOR ANY ENGINE: dividing sunset→sunrise and sunrise→sunset into twelve equal parts is the MODERN seasonal-hour convention. Nothing in this ledger attests it as an Egyptian procedure; what the ledger attests is a per-month table read off a water clock and a set of star risings that every source here agrees were uneven. If the site computes equal twelfths it must label them as the modern convention and not as the Egyptian one.
polarBehaviour: NOT ATTESTED, AND THE SYSTEM AS ATTESTED DOES NOT TRANSFER. Nothing in this ledger addresses any latitude outside Egypt (roughly 22°–32° N). The night-hour count as attested is not a computation over an arbitrary sunset/sunrise pair: it is a reading taken off a physical vessel whose twelve month-scales were cut for one place [S8-f, S10-c], and off decan risings that Symons is reported to have shown were uneven even in Egypt [S10-a, S10-b]. The only season-length problem the ledger contains is Budge's own — that the Egyptian summer night is not twelve hours long — and his answer is that divisions I and XII are ante-chambers, which is a statement about the book and not about the sky [S3-c]. Above the polar circles a sunset/sunrise pair may not exist at all; this ledger says nothing whatever about that case. Whatever the engine does there is the engine's convention and must be labelled as the engine's, not as Egyptian.

entries.note: Budge, Gods of the Egyptians II (Chicago/London 1904), ch. XIX §V, p. 294, heads a list 'The Gods and Goddesses of the Hours of the Day' numbered from 'First Hour' to 'Twelfth Hour'. In the Internet Archive OCR the two printed columns are flattened: the twelve hour-labels print as one block and the twelve names as another. The fetcher records that the order of the names is as shown and runs 1–12, but that the pairing of a name to an hour number is read off column order and was not seen stated on any single line — so the NAME is attested and the PAIRING is not. Budge gives no source for this list or for the three other hour-lists in the same chapter (§VI, §XI, §XII), while the adjacent planet list (§XIII) and dekan list (§XIV) both carry footnotes to Brugsch and Lepsius. That asymmetry is recorded rather than explained.

entries.name: Urt-em-sekhemu-s — 1906 witness only; unverified against the Amduat itself
entries.note: Fourth Division of the Tuat. Budge's third volume (1906) supplies what his first (1905) does not. The summary list at p. 97 gives Division IV the name Ankhet-kheperu, the gate Ament-Sethau and the hour-goddess Urt-em-sekhemu-s; the running text at p. 132 gives the same gate and the same goddess. The two 1906 witnesses agree with each other exactly. THE PROBLEM IS ELSEWHERE: Budge's own 1905 volume has no hour-name here at all — the fetcher ran the pattern 'name of (the|this) (hour)' over all twelve chapter files of the vol. I transcription and it matches in Divisions II, VII, VIII, IX, X, XI and XII and nowhere else. Whether the Amduat itself names this hour and Budge omitted it in 1905, or whether the 1906 name comes from elsewhere, cannot be settled from this ledger: Hornung's Texte zum Amduat is the critical edition that would settle it and was not obtained (it is also in copyright and could not be quoted if it were). This cell is therefore attributed to Budge 1906 and to nobody else.

Gods of the same twelve hours: Khepera, Ab-em-tu-f, Neb-xeteru (almost certainly Neb-neteru), An-mut-f, Bapi-f, Heru-sbati, Seker, Hertt-her-kiiet (unresolved), Maa-hra, Pesh-hetep-f, Ka-taui, Ka-khu — quoted as the extraction prints them, corruptions and all.
variants.note: None of these names matches the Am-Tuat night series recorded in the entries table. So one author, in works published within two years of each other, transmits at least three unrelated night-hour name-sets: the Am-Tuat goddesses (1905/1906), this §XI series (1904), and §VI's assertion that the night deities are simply the day deities over again. Nothing in this ledger reconciles them and this dossier does not try.

variants.label: Budge 1904 §VI (p. 294) — the night hours carry the same names as the day hours, in the same order
positions: §VI is a single sentence in substance: the deities of the hours of the night are the same as those of the hours of the day, and their names follow each other in the same order.
variants.note: Recorded because it contradicts §XI on the facing pages of the same chapter, and contradicts the Am-Tuat series entirely. If §VI is taken at face value the day-hour names in entries 1–12 are also the night-hour names — which the Am-Tuat flatly is not. Kept unresolved.

variants.label: The Book of Gates divides the Tuat into twelve WITHOUT hour-names
positions: Budge 1906, p. 100: the divisions of the Tuat according to the Book of Gates are usually marked by Gates guarded by serpents. The fetcher records, as evidence of looking, that the summary of the Book of Gates at pp. 100–102 lists a serpent name and a gate name for each of the twelve divisions and NO hour-goddess: twelve divisions, zero hour-names.

Budge 1906, at about p. 140, on the Book of Gates: the Hour-goddesses are the daughters of Ra ('Ea' in the extraction, the habitual misreading) and their work is to guide their father through the night; six of them represent the first six hours and the other six the last six. Budge adds that in the Book of Gates the twelve are depicted together, whereas in the Book Am-Tuat each appears in the Hour to which she belongs.
variants.note: Two different books of the same underworld divide the night into twelve differently: the Am-Tuat attaches a named goddess to each hour, the Book of Gates groups twelve goddesses six-and-six and names the divisions by their serpents and gates instead. Any page presenting 'the' Egyptian night hours is choosing a book.

variants.label: Budge 1906 contradicts himself about whether the Am-Tuat divisions have gates at all
positions: Budge 1906, p. 102: from the preceding lists it is clear that in the Book Am-Tuat the actual divisions of the Tuat are considered without any reference to Gates.
Budge 1906, pp. 97–98: his own Am-Tuat summary, four pages earlier, prints gate-names for divisions IV onwards — Ament-Sethau, Aha-neteru, Sept-Metu and the rest.
variants.note: Recorded as-is and not reconciled. It bears directly on how much weight the gate-names in the entries table can carry.

variants.label: The Internet Sacred Text Archive transcription of Budge 1905 is not a faithful witness to the printed book
positions: The transcription reproduces the chapter headings at pp. 139 and 256 uncorrected — 'THEPHET-ASAR' and 'THEN-NETERU' — which are precisely the two lines Budge's own printed errata leaf corrects to 'Thephet-shetat' and 'Kheper-kekiu-khau-mestu'.
The transcription's own errata.htm is, in its entirety, a note that 'againt' on page 140 should read 'against'. It does not reproduce Budge's printed errata at all.
Budge's printed Contents at pp. vii–viii already carries the corrected forms, so the printed book disagrees with itself between Contents and chapter heading before any transcription is involved.
variants.note: PRACTICAL WARNING FOR ANYONE EXTENDING THIS DOSSIER: reading hour and division names off chapter headings in the online transcription will import two known errors that the author of the book personally corrected in 1905. Read the running text and the Contents, and check the errata leaf in the Internet Archive scan.

variants.label: Cassius Dio's Egyptian attribution of the planetary hour-rotation
positions: Dio, Roman History 37.18.1 (trans. Cary, Loeb 1914): referring the days to the seven planets was instituted by the Egyptians and is now found among all mankind.
Dio, immediately following: its adoption has been comparatively recent, and the ancient Greeks never understood it so far as he is aware.

Dio 37.19.1–2: begin at the first hour and count the hours of day and night, assigning the first to Saturn, according to the order of the cycles the Egyptians observe, and repeat — which generates the weekday sequence.
variants.note: THIS IS THE ONLY TEXT IN THE LEDGER THAT ATTACHES HOUR-RULERS TO THE WORD 'EGYPTIANS', AND IT IS NOT ENOUGH TO BUILD A COLUMN ON. Dio writes in the early third century AD, in Greek, calls the practice recent, and names no Egyptian hour, no Egyptian hour-name and no Egyptian source. It is evidence about the Roman-period planetary week and about what a Roman senator believed of its origin. See rulerColumnJustification and gaps[0].

variants.label: Brugsch prints day-hour material this ledger could not read
positions: Brugsch, Thesaurus Inscriptionum Aegyptiacarum I (1883), contents: 'Die Sonne in den 12 Stunden des Tages', p. 57 — a treatment of the sun in the twelve hours of the DAY, which is the layer this dossier is thinnest on.
The same contents lists the hour-tables from the tombs of Ramesses VI and Ramesses IX at Thebes.

One clean passage in the printed preface material dates the Sirius epoch to the eleventh hour of the night of the fifth epagomenal day, going into the New Year's day of 1 Thoth of the fixed year — an hour of the night used as a real chronological coordinate.
variants.note: NO HOUR NAME IS QUOTED FROM BRUGSCH AND NONE MAY BE. The volume is autographed — Brugsch hand-drew the plates and their German captions — so the Google OCR of the hour tables at about pp. 47–60 is unrecoverable. Only the printed contents lines were legible. This entry exists so that a human knows exactly which page to open. It is also the upstream source Budge cites for his planet and dekan lists (Thesaurus pp. 65 ff., 137 ff.) and which Griffith & Thompson cite at p. 68.

goldenValues.label: Karnak clepsydra — longest month-scale to shortest, 14 fingers to 12

contestedPoints: WHETHER TENT-BAIU NAMES THE THIRD HOUR. Budge 1905 (vol. I, p. 50) says only that the god paddles TOWARDS the Hour Tent-baiu and never calls it the third hour's name; Budge 1906 (vol. III, p. 121) states that the goddess of the hour called Tent-baiu has taken charge of the Boat, in his Third Division chapter. One author, two volumes, one year apart. Both kept. [S2-c vs S3-g]

WHETHER THE AM-TUAT NAMES HOURS FOUR, FIVE AND SIX AT ALL. Budge's 1905 volume has no hour-name formula in those three chapters — established by pattern scan over all twelve chapter files, not by impression. Budge's 1906 volume supplies a goddess for each, twice over. Whether the Amduat itself names them and the 1905 volume omitted them, or whether the 1906 names come from another witness, cannot be settled here: Hornung's Texte zum Amduat is the critical edition that would settle it, was not obtained, and is in copyright. These three cells are attributed to Budge 1906 and to nobody else. [S2-j, S3-d, S3-e, S3-f, S3-h, S3-i, S3-j]

THE FIFTH DIVISION'S GODDESS: Sekmet-her-abt-uaa-s (Budge 1906 summary list, p. 97) against SEMix-HER-ABT-uiA-s (Budge 1906 running text, ~p. 135, as the extraction prints it — an OCR corruption of the printed form, probably SEMIT- or SEKMET-). Recorded unresolved; the fetcher explicitly declined to choose and so does this dossier. [S3-e vs S3-i]

THE SEVENTH DIVISION'S NAME, GATE AND GODDESS, three separate divergences at one locus: Thephet-Asar / Thephet-sheta / Thephet-shetat for the division, corrected by Budge's own printed errata; Ruti-Asar / Kuti-Asar / Ruti-en-Asar for the gate; Kheftes-Hau-hesq-Neha-hra / Khesfet-hau-hesqetu-neha-hra for the goddess. [S1-a, S1-b, S2-d, S2-f, S3-k]
THE SIXTH DIVISION'S NAME: Metchet-nebt-Tuat (summary) against Metchet-mu-nebt-Tuat (running text), with the gate broken as 'Sept-' in one and completed as 'Sept-Metu' in the other. [S3-f vs S3-j]

WHETHER THE AM-TUAT DIVISIONS HAVE GATES. Budge 1906 p. 102 says the Am-Tuat divisions are considered without any reference to Gates; his own summary at pp. 97–98 prints gate-names for divisions IV onwards. Unreconciled by him and unreconciled here. [S3-q vs S3-d, S3-e, S3-f]

WHICH CIVIL MONTH HAS THE SHORTEST NIGHT, AND THEREFORE HOW OLD THE KARNAK CLOCK IS. Parker §208: month ten (II šmw). Schomberg, reported by Brack-Bernsen: month nine, which would make the clock some 250 years older. [S8-g vs S10-d, S10-e]

WHETHER THE KARNAK SCALES BELONG TO AMENHOTEP III'S REIGN. Parker's notes to ch. V, n. 73, report that the scale markings cannot be reconciled with the reign in which the vessel was made, around 1400 BC, and that Borchardt dated them instead to ca. 1630–1510 BC; Parker himself reads the mismatch as Egyptian conservatism rather than as a redating. Two readings of one mismatch. [S8-j]

WHETHER DECAN-BASED NIGHT DIVISION WAS EVER A WORKING CLOCK. Brack-Bernsen reports Symons demonstrating that no set of real stars can both make its first dawn appearance on the required day and come up at evenly spaced moments, so what the decans marked out was unequal; Ainsworth judges it improbable that the transit-decan instruments served the living for telling time as it passed, and notes the charts served the dead. Against that stands the plain fact that hours were used as appointment times — Parker's Dendera procession at the arrival of the third hour, and Brugsch's Sirius epoch in the eleventh hour of the night. [S10-a, S10-b, S9-b, S9-d vs S8-l, S7-c]

WHERE THE EGYPTIAN DAY BEGINS. Parker §32 reports dawn, on three earlier scholars' demonstration; Parker's own notes to ch. I, n. 17, record a second boundary in the same civilisation, the pre-sunrise light belonging to the preceding day in the astronomical reckoning and to the new day in ordinary usage; and the night-hour instrument starts at sunset regardless. Three boundaries; this dossier reconciles none of them. [S8-a, S8-b, S8-d, S8-e]

WHETHER 'THE EGYPTIANS' OF THE PLANETARY HOUR-ROTATION ARE EGYPTIANS IN ANY PHARAONIC SENSE. Dio 37.18–19 credits it to them and calls it comparatively recent, writing in the early third century AD and naming no Egyptian hour or source; nothing in the Egyptian-language material in this ledger — Budge's four hour-lists, the Am-Tuat, the Demotic magical papyrus — assigns a planet to an hour. [S6-a, S6-b, S6-c, S6-d vs S4-g, S5-a, S5-e]

honestLimits: WHAT THIS DOSSIER IS WORTH, STATED PLAINLY. (1) IT IS BUDGE ALL THE WAY DOWN. Every Egyptian hour-name in the entries table — all twelve day names and all ten night names that have one — comes from E. A. Wallis Budge, in three volumes published 1904–1906, read through Internet Archive OCR and a third-party HTML transcription. There is no second author anywhere in the name data. This is FRAMING §4.4 operating exactly as that section predicts: the public-domain constraint selects the worst witnesses, and here it selects one witness. Hornung's Texte zum Amduat is the critical edition that would settle the three real questions (do hours 4–6 have names in the Amduat; which reading of the Fifth Division's goddess is right; is Tent-baiu the third hour); it is in copyright, could not be quoted under §4 even if obtained, and was not attempted. Jéquier 1894 would break the Budge monopoly cheaply and was not obtained. (2) THE DAY HOURS REST ON ONE UNSOURCED LIST IN A POPULAR COMPENDIUM, READ OFF A FLATTENED COLUMN. Budge's §V gives twelve names and the fetcher confirms their order runs 1–12, but the pairing of name to hour number was read from column order in an OCR that merged two printed columns, and was not seen stated on any line. Budge gives no source for §V, §VI, §XI or §XII, while the planet list and dekan list on the very next pages both footnote Brugsch and Lepsius. That asymmetry is in the ledger and is not explained away here. Every one of those twelve entries carries the caveat in its own name field, so a renderer that shows only the name still shows the caveat. (3) THE §XII DAY LIST IS DELIBERATELY NOT DISTRIBUTED. Budge prints a second, incompatible twelve-name day list at p. 302; the fetcher could not read hour-to-goddess-to-god triples off it and said so; it is recorded whole in variants and no rows are built from it. Two incompatible day lists in one chapter is a finding about the source, and flattening it into one tidy table would destroy the finding. (4) TWO NIGHT CELLS ARE EMPTY AND THAT IS CORRECT. Divisions IX and X carry an hour-name in the witness — the pattern scan proves it — but no snippet captured the wording, so no name is entered. The cheapest fix in the whole dossier is to open bat12.htm and bat13.htm. (5) THE RULER COLUMN IS EMPTY AND THE EMPTINESS IS THE TEACHING. Round 1 filled it with Am-Tuat hour-goddesses on a system whose own scope note says it has no rulers. An hour-goddess in a funerary cosmography is not a lord in a rotating planetary sequence, and four independent lines of ledger evidence say the Egyptian material does not have the second thing (see rulerColumnJustification). Cassius Dio's attribution is real and is recorded in variants, and it is an attribution made in Greek, in the third century AD, by a writer who calls the practice recent and names no Egyptian anything. (6) THE THREE MODERN SOURCES ARE CITE-ONLY AND ARE PARAPHRASED THROUGHOUT. Parker 1950, Ainsworth 2018 and Brack-Bernsen's BMCR review are in copyright; no verbatim text from any of them appears in this file, and the sources[] entries for their snippets carry a paraphrase with a pointer to the fetcher ledger rather than the words. Budge (1904, 1905, 1906), Griffith & Thompson (1904), Brugsch (1883) and Cary's Loeb Dio (1914) are public domain in the United States on the pre-1930 threshold stated in FRAMING §4.3, and are the only sources quoted. (7) EVERYTHING SYMONS OR SCHOMBERG IS SAID TO ARGUE IS SECOND-HAND. The Brill volume was not obtainable, so those positions are attributable to Brack-Bernsen reporting them and to nobody else, and are labelled that way at every occurrence. (8) NOTHING HERE SUPPORTS AN EQUAL-TWELFTHS ENGINE AS AN EGYPTIAN PROCEDURE. The twelve are attested; the equal division is not, anywhere in this ledger. If the site computes sunset-to-sunrise divided by twelve it is applying a modern seasonal-hour convention to Egyptian names, and the page must say so in its own voice. attemptedAndFailed.cite: Ludwig Borchardt, 'Die altägyptische Zeitmessung', in Ernst von Bassermann-Jordan, Die Geschichte der Zeitmessung und der Uhren, Bd. I,B (Berlin, 1920)
attemptedAndFailed.why: Not digitised anywhere reachable: two Internet Archive advanced-search queries each returned an EMPTY result set. Published 1920, so it would be public domain and quotable if found. It matters twice over — Parker's source for the 12:14 finger ratio (S8-i) and for the ca. 1630–1510 B.C. redating (S8-j), and the principal pre-1930 treatment of Egyptian SHADOW clocks, i.e. the day-hour instrument this dossier still has nothing on.

attemptedAndFailed.cite: Gustave Jéquier, Le Livre de ce qu'il y a dans l'Hadès (1894) — second public-domain edition of the abridged Amduat
attemptedAndFailed.why: Not re-attempted this round and still outstanding from round 1, where the download URL mis-encoded the accented filename and returned a 404 page. It would corroborate or isolate Budge's hour-names independently, which is exactly what the divergences between S2, S3 and S4 call for. THE HIGHEST-VALUE OUTSTANDING FETCH IN THIS DOSSIER.

Not attempted, and recorded so the omission is visible rather than silent. It is in copyright and under FRAMING §4 could not be quoted even if obtained; it is the critical edition that would settle whether hours 4, 5 and 6 have names in the Amduat itself, as against Budge's two conflicting Edwardian renderings. Its absence is why those three cells are attributed to Budge 1906 and to nobody else.
